064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy: The Rolling Stones are the British rock band behind 'Paint It, Black', 'Gimme Shelter', and 'Sympathy for the Devil', famous for their blues-rooted swagger and for still touring into their seventies. A band proud of its anti-intellectual image turns out to raise real philosophical questions: what a song or a band actually is when every performance changes it, whether genius can exist only in a partnership like Mick Jagger and Keith Richards, what it means to keep searching for satisfaction, and how a devil's-eye view of evil holds up.
065 - Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy -: Chuck Klosterman is an American essayist whose 2000s books, such as Sex, Drugs, and Cocoa Puffs and Killing Yourself to Live, made a name for treating rock bands, sports, cereal, and sitcoms with lethal seriousness. His trademark question — whether 'guilty pleasures' make any sense, or whether nothing is ever just itself — invites philosophy at a busy intersection: Kant on perspective, Kierkegaard on irony, Nietzsche on masks, and honest puzzles about self-knowledge, tribute bands, and whether culture itself can be wrong.
066 - Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods: Neil Gaiman is the British author of American Gods, Coraline, and The Sandman comics, beloved for fantasy in which ordinary people stumble into hidden worlds ruled by old stories. That premise is a philosopher's playground: gods who exist only because people believe in them raise questions about what belief and personhood are; con-men gods staging 'coincidences' test Hume on causation; Plato's case against poetry gets answered by Aristotle; and Gaiman's dream realm asks whether our nightly dreams might be visits to a real place.
067 - Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badd: Breaking Bad is the acclaimed AMC drama (2008-2013) in which Walter White, a high-school chemistry teacher with cancer, starts cooking methamphetamine and slowly becomes a monster. The show is a deliberate morality play in the line of Macbeth and Faust, and the questions follow naturally: what really drove Walt, how we should grade each of his killings, whether a strict materialist can have a soul, whether 'Heisenberg' is a lie or an authentic self, and what doctors and families owe a dying man's choices.
068 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy -: The Walking Dead is the hugely popular comic and AMC series about survivors of a zombie apocalypse, where law, government, and property are gone and the dead walk as mindless 'walkers'. The premise works as a philosophy laboratory: Hobbes's state of nature becomes a question about how survivors should treat each other, while the walkers themselves probe consciousness, personal identity, knowledge, and personhood — and force the uncomfortable question of whether killing a walker is murder or mercy.
069 - Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosoph: Curb Your Enthusiasm is the long-running HBO sitcom in which Seinfeld co-creator Larry David plays a wealthy, tactless version of himself who says what everyone else suppresses. Because the show runs on unwritten social rules and what happens when one man ignores them, it invites philosophy from several directions: classic theories of humor, Heidegger and Wittgenstein on the background practices nobody notices, whether civility's rules can be justified, what Larry's devoted idleness is worth, and whether the Larry on screen is a character or the man.
070 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosoph: Dungeons and Dragons, created by Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson in 1974, is the tabletop role-playing game where friends gather around dice and imagination to tell fantasy stories together. That setup turns out to be fertile philosophical ground: what kind of thing a game even is, whether playing is mere escapism or genuine art, whether playing an evil character convincingly refutes virtue ethics, how the nine-fold alignment system maps onto Kant and Mill, and why losing a beloved character can hurt like real grief.
072 - Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is: Jeopardy! is America's most famous quiz show, running since 1964 on its signature gimmick: contestants are given answers and must phrase their responses as questions. A game built entirely on facts and wagers is surprisingly deep territory: what knowledge is and whether the judges own it, whether the game is genuinely fair or a portrait of American meritocracy, what makes a game good at all in Bernard Suits's sense, and what IBM's Watson victory over champions like Ken Jennings says about thinking machines.
073 - The Wire and Philosophy - This Ame: The Wire is the HBO crime drama (2002-2008) that followed the police, drug dealers, dockworkers, politicians, schoolchildren, and journalists of Baltimore, and is widely regarded as one of television's great novels. Its sweep raises sweeping questions: how post-industrial capitalism quietly devalues whole neighborhoods, whether the drug trade's 'Game' traps everyone in a rigged cycle, what it means that some Americans live with rights only on paper, and whether a father's partiality or an impartial moral code better explains the show's best and worst moments.
074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy: Planet of the Apes began with the 1968 film in which astronaut Charlton Heston crash-lands on a world where articulate apes rule and mute humans are animals — and it continues today with the Rise prequels about the intelligent chimp Caesar. The reversal does real philosophical work: Taylor in the dock replays Galileo's trial, Zira's lab dissections echo Descartes's beast-machine doctrine, and the films press hard questions about other minds, whether language or deception is the true test of personhood, and the ethics of enhancing animals.
